query: We are investigating the anomalous ductile-brittle-ductile transition in an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA aged in the 550-750°C regime. The baseline as-cast material is ductile. Aging at ~600°C induces a brittle state characterized by a loss of elongation, while aging at ~750°C restores ductility. The failure mechanism is hypothesized to stem from the coupled evolution of L12 ordered domains and jagged phase boundaries, distinct from conventional temper embrittlement. Specifically, the hypothesis is that excessive ordering (near stoichiometric Ni3Al ratios) within the FCC matrix, combined with jagged B2/FCC interfaces, creates a high antiphase boundary energy (APBE) and restricts cross-slip, leading to planar slip and stress concentration at boundary serrations. Conversely, higher aging temperatures reduce the order degree and form ductile transition zones along the PBs. Formulate a hypothesis detailing the specific atomic-scale mechanism (e.g., APBE changes, SISFE modulation) driving the brittle window. What is the critical boundary for the transition in terms of chemical ordering? Propose a falsification experiment using nanoindentation or transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to distinguish this mechanism from simple phase decomposition, and predict the specific structural feature (e.g., jagged PBs) that must be observed to confirm the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The brittle window in AlCoCrFeNi2.1 HEA aged at 600°C is caused by the synergistic effect of high-order L12 precipitates (approaching stoichiometric Ni3Al) and jagged B2/FCC phase boundaries, which elevate the antiphase boundary energy (APBE) and suppress cross-slip, forcing planar slip and stress concentration at boundary serrations; this effect is reversed at 750°C where reduced ordering and the formation of ductile transition zones along the boundaries restore ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a ductile FCC matrix and B2 phase, exhibiting high ductility and no significant ordering.
generation.intervention: Isothermal aging at 600°C for a duration sufficient to induce L12 ordering and boundary serration, followed by a comparative aging at 750°C.
generation.conditions: Aging temperatures between 550°C and 750°C, specifically targeting the 600°C brittle regime and 750°C ductile regime.
generation.structural_mediator: Jagged B2/FCC phase boundaries and L12 ordered domains within the FCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: At 600°C, excessive chemical ordering increases the antiphase boundary energy (APBE) of the L12 precipitates. Combined with the geometric stress concentrators at jagged phase boundaries, this restricts dislocation cross-slip, promoting planar slip and localized stress accumulation that leads to brittle fracture. At 750°C, thermal energy reduces the degree of ordering and promotes the formation of ductile transition zones along the boundaries, mitigating the APBE effect and allowing cross-slip.
generation.predicted_outcome: Aging at 600°C will result in a significant drop in elongation (brittle state) correlated with high APBE and jagged boundaries, while aging at 750°C will restore elongation (ductile state) with reduced ordering and smoother or transition-zone-modified boundaries.
generation.baseline: As-cast ductile AlCoCrFeNi2.1 HEA with no L12 ordering and smooth phase boundaries.
generation.boundary: The transition occurs when the degree of L12 ordering exceeds a critical threshold (near stoichiometric Ni3Al ratios) and the phase boundary morphology becomes sufficiently jagged to induce planar slip, a condition met at ~600°C but not at ~750°C.
generation.uncertainty: The exact critical threshold for the degree of ordering (e.g., specific superlattice intensity or Ni/Al ratio) required to trigger the brittle transition is not quantified in the provided evidence. Additionally, the precise contribution of jagged boundary geometry versus APBE alone to the stress concentration is not isolated in the available literature.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform in-situ transmission electron microscopy (TEM) tensile testing on AlCoCrFeNi2.1 samples aged at 600°C (brittle) and 750°C (ductile). Simultaneously, use nanoindentation with high spatial resolution to map the local mechanical properties across the B2/FCC phase boundaries and within the FCC matrix.
measurements: Dislocation slip character (planar vs. wavy) observed via TEM during deformation.
Local yield strength and hardness gradients across jagged vs. smooth phase boundaries via nanoindentation.
Antiphase boundary energy (APBE) estimation via superlattice streak intensity analysis in selected area diffraction patterns (SADP).
Phase boundary morphology (jaggedness factor) quantified via high-resolution STEM imaging.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if: (1) Samples aged at 600°C exhibit wavy slip and cross-slip activity despite high L12 ordering and jagged boundaries, or (2) Samples aged at 750°C exhibit planar slip and brittle fracture despite reduced ordering, or (3) No correlation is found between the degree of L12 ordering (APBE proxy) and the transition from wavy to planar slip.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have attracted a lot of attention in recent years, due to the unique combinations of structural, physical and chemical properties of these alloys [1] – [3] . HEAs usually form simple structures such as body-centered cubic (BCC) (e.g. TaNbHfZrTi [4] , NbTaVWZr [5] etc.) or face-centered cubic (FCC) (e.g., CoCrCuFeNi [6] , CoCrFeMnNi [7] etc.) solid solutions. The large number of the alloying elements in near-equiatomic proportions result in high configurational entropy in these solid solutions. However, these alloys can decompose to multiple phases upon changing the composition or annealing at different temperatures or a combination of both [8] – [10] . Such a phase decomposition is often the result of the complex interplay of configurational entropy of mixing with the enthalpies of mixing of the constituent elements. Additionally, such multiphase microstructures are more likely to exhibit the desired properties for real engineering applications. Hence, tuning the composition and fractions of phases is critical for achieving the desired properties [10] , [11] .
